slice/two: So far, every function had one input. This one has two, u and v, so picture it as ground: each spot is a pair of inputs, and the height there is the output, f.
slice/rings: Seen from above, like a hiking map, each ring joins spots of equal height. They rise away from the middle: a bowl.
slice/which: Stand at the point one, one. How steep is it here? That depends on which way you step: along u, the ground climbs at one rate, and along v, at another.
slice/hold: So move one input at a time. Hold v at one and let only u move: you walk along this dashed line, and the heights along it trace an ordinary curve.
slice/f: This bowl is f of u and v equals u squared plus two v squared. With v held at one, two v squared is a fixed two, so the curve is u squared, plus two.
slice/slope: Differentiate it as usual. u squared gives two u, and the constant two gives zero. At u equals one, the slope is two.
slice/partial: That slope is the partial derivative of f in u: partial, because it counts only the part of f's change that comes from u.
slice/curly: It is written partial f, partial u, with a curly d, read “partial”. Here it is two.
slice/legendre: Adrien-Marie Legendre wrote it this way in 1786, he said, to avoid any ambiguity: the curly d marks a slope where only one input moves.
slice/jacobi: Legendre later dropped it. Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi took it up again in 1841, to tell partial derivatives from ordinary ones at a glance, and it stuck.
other/hold: Now hold u at one instead, and let only v move. The line runs up the page, and along it the curve is one, plus two v squared.
other/dv: Two v squared gives four v, and the constant one gives zero. So partial f, partial v is four v: four, at v equals one.
other/steep: That is twice as steep as along u, and the map shows it: the rings crowd closer together this way.
other/rule: So a partial is an ordinary derivative, with every other input frozen at a number. A term without the moving input is a constant, and gives zero.
other/one: With a single input, there is nothing to hold still, and the partial is just the derivative, f prime. The curly d only says that other inputs exist, and stay where they are.
mixed/mix: Some terms mix the inputs. Take f of u and v equals u squared plus three u v, at the point u equals one, v equals two.
mixed/held: For the partial in u, walk the slice where v is two. There, three u v is three times two times u: six u, a line in u with slope six.
mixed/pu: So a held v is just a number multiplying u, and three u v gives three v. With u squared giving two u, partial f, partial u is two u plus three v: two plus six, eight.
mixed/pv: For the partial in v, walk the slice where u is one. u squared is a constant there, giving zero, and three u v gives three u: three.
worked/p: Try one. f of u and v equals u squared v, plus two v squared, plus three u. What is partial f, partial u at two, one?
worked/du: Hold v. u squared v is v times u squared, so it gives v times two u: two u v. Two v squared gives zero, and three u gives three.
worked/du-n: At two, one: two times two times one is four, plus three, seven.
worked/q: And partial f, partial v at the same point?
worked/dv: Hold u. u squared v is u squared times v, so it gives u squared. Two v squared gives four v, and three u gives zero.
worked/dv-n: Two squared is four, plus four times one: eight.
